section_1.title: Prerequisites: Vectors and Planes
section_1.content: Briefly define vectors as directed line segments with magnitude and direction. Remind students of the Right-Hand Rule (RHR) and the concept of an orthogonal vector (a vector perpendicular to a plane).
section_1.example: Visualizing a flat sheet of paper (a plane) and a pencil standing straight up at 90 degrees to represent the normal vector.

section_2.title: The 2D Pseudo-Cross Product
section_2.content: Explain that while the cross product is strictly a 3D operation, in 2D we use a scalar 'perp product' (x1y2 - y1x2) to find the signed area of a parallelogram. It indicates orientation (clockwise vs counter-clockwise).
section_2.example: A robotic arm on a 2D plane: calculating the 'perp product' of two joint vectors to determine if the arm needs to turn left or right to reach an object.

section_3.title: The 3D Cross Product: Definition and Geometric Meaning
section_3.content: Introduce the cross product as an operation resulting in a vector. Key property: The result is perpendicular to both input vectors. Its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram formed by the two vectors.
section_3.example: Animation of a butterfly flapping its wings: The cross product vector acts as the 'axis' of the wing's rotation, pointing directly outward.

section_4.title: Computational Method: The Determinant
section_4.content: Demonstrate the algebraic calculation using the 3x3 matrix determinant method. Show how the unit vectors i, j, and k organize the components of vectors A and B.
section_4.example: Calculating the cross product of Vector A (1, 2, 3) and Vector B (4, 5, 6) using the 'expanding along the top row' technique.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: Torque
section_5.content: Conclude with the physics application of the cross product: Torque (τ = r × F). Explain how the cross product determines the direction of rotation when a force is applied to a lever arm.
section_5.example: A mechanic using a wrench: the cross product of the wrench's length vector and the force vector applied to the handle shows exactly which way the bolt will rotate.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.0 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
